children: Paraguay’s former president, Santiago Peña, was brought before prosecutors Saturday after Congress removed him from office amid a banking crisis that has blocked millions of customers from accessing their money, the Associated Press reported.

For investors, Ueno Bank’s collapse raises questions about banking oversight, the recovery of government funds and the new administration’s ability to restore confidence. Reimbursements could help ease tensions, while prolonged disruption and protests could weigh on economic activity.
Prosecutors ordered the arrests of Peña and former Central Bank chief Carlos Carvallo on Friday in an investigation into alleged breach of trust and other offenses connected to the failed lender.
Lawmakers accuse Peña of directing hundreds of millions of dollars in public money into Ueno while regulators failed to address risky lending to insiders. He denies wrongdoing.

The Senate unanimously voted to remove Peña three days after authorities seized the bank, cutting off nearly 3 million customers from their accounts. Vice President Pedro Alliana succeeded him and began appointing ministers Saturday.
The Central Bank said 1.2 million customers had recovered some or all of their insured deposits by Saturday.
Peña offered to resign Thursday, but lawmakers pursued impeachment instead, seeking to prevent him from retaining immunity after leaving office.
The crisis has sparked demonstrations and confrontations with police. Paraguay’s largest teachers’ union plans an indefinite strike beginning Monday to demand safeguards for public pension funds.
